`<form>` collects user input. Key attributes:
- `action="URL"` — where the data is sent
- `method="GET"` (data in URL) or `"POST"` (data in body)

  <textarea id="msg" name="message"></textarea>

**Essentials (every page):**

- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` — mobile responsive

**SEO basics:**
- `<title>` — appears as the headline in Google results (~60 chars)

```html
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>My Article — Site Name</title>
  <meta name="description" content="A 160-char summary for Google.">
```

Summary:
**Accessibility (a11y)** ensures everyone — including users with visual, hearing, motor, or cognitive disabilities — can use your site.

**Core principles (mostly free if you do them right):**

1. **Semantic HTML** (Section 1.6) does 80% of the work automatically — `<button>` is keyboard-accessible by default; a styled `<div>` is not.
2. **`alt` text** on images (Section 1.4) — required.
3. **`<label>` for form inputs** (Section 1.5) — required.
4. **Keyboard navigation** — every interactive element must be reachable via Tab and activated via Enter/Space.
5. **`aria-label`** / **`aria-labelledby`** — adds an accessible name to elements that lack visible text (e.g. icon-only buttons).
6. **`role="..."`** — adds semantic meaning when the native tag can't (rare; prefer semantic HTML first).
7. **Color contrast** — normal text needs ≥ **4.5:1** contrast ratio against background (WCAG AA).
8. **Heading hierarchy** (Section 1.2) — sequential, no skipping.

**Test with:**
- Chrome Lighthouse (built-in audit)
- axe DevTools extension
- Real screen readers: VoiceOver (Mac), NVDA (Windows)

Summary:
Every HTML element is a **box** with 4 layers (inside to outside):

1. **Content** — the actual text/image
2. **Padding** — space INSIDE the border, around content
3. **Border** — line around padding
4. **Margin** — space OUTSIDE the border, between elements

**Default `box-sizing: content-box`** is annoying: setting `width: 200px` only sizes the CONTENT — padding/border ADD to total width. So a 200px wide box with 20px padding becomes 240px total.

**Always add this reset** at top of CSS:
```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```

With `border-box`, `width: 200px` INCLUDES padding and border. Total stays 200px. Much easier to reason about.

`margin` collapses vertically (two stacked elements: smaller margin disappears). `padding` never collapses.

Summary:
Flexbox is a 1-dimensional layout system — perfect for rows or columns. Set `display: flex` on the PARENT to make it a flex container. All direct children become flex items automatically.

**Container properties (on parent):**
- `flex-direction: row | column` — main axis direction (default `row`)
- `justify-content: flex-start | center | space-between | space-around | space-evenly` — aligns along MAIN axis
- `align-items: stretch | flex-start | center | flex-end` — aligns along CROSS axis
- `flex-wrap: nowrap | wrap` — single line or wrap to multiple
- `gap: 1rem` — spacing between items (better than margins)

**Item properties (on children):**
- `flex: 1` shorthand for `flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0`
- `align-self` — override `align-items` for individual item

```css
.nav { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; gap: 1rem; }
```

Summary:
Grid is a 2-dimensional layout system — for rows AND columns simultaneously. Set `display: grid` on the parent.

**Key properties:**
- `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr` — 3 equal columns (`fr` = fractional unit of available space)
- `grid-template-rows: 100px auto` — explicit row sizes
- `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)` — shorthand for 3 columns of 1fr
- `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` — responsive grid, items reflow based on container width
- `gap: 1rem` — spacing between grid cells
- `grid-column: 1 / 3` (on item) — span columns 1 to 3

**Grid vs Flexbox:** Use Grid for 2D layouts (page layout, card galleries). Use Flexbox for 1D (navigation, button rows).

```css
.gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
```

Summary:
The `position` property controls how an element is placed:

- **`static`** (default) — normal document flow. `top/right/bottom/left` have NO effect.
- **`relative`** — same position in flow, but `top/right/bottom/left` shift it visually (other elements still see original spot). Often used to create a positioning context for absolute children.
- **`absolute`** — REMOVED from normal flow. Positioned relative to nearest ancestor with `position: relative` (or to viewport if none). Other elements ignore it.
- **`fixed`** — positioned relative to the VIEWPORT (always visible, even when scrolling). Useful for sticky headers, chat widgets.
- **`sticky`** — acts like `relative` until you scroll past it, then becomes `fixed`. Great for table headers that stick at the top.

`z-index: N` controls stacking order (higher = on top) — only works on positioned elements.

A **merge conflict** happens when Git can't auto-merge changes because two branches modified the same lines.

**When you see this:**
```

your version
=======
their version
>>>>>>> feat/their-branch
```

**Resolve manually:**
1. Open conflicted file in editor (VS Code highlights conflicts)

**Avoid conflicts:**
- Pull often (`git pull` regularly)
- Keep branches short-lived
- Communicate with teammates about who's editing what
- Use small focused PRs

JavaScript has 3 ways to declare variables:

- **`const`** — value can't be reassigned. USE THIS BY DEFAULT.
- **`let`** — value CAN be reassigned. Use ONLY when reassignment is needed.
- **`var`** — old. AVOID. Has function scope (vs block scope of let/const) — causes confusing bugs.

```js
const PI = 3.14;
PI = 3.15;  // TypeError

let count = 0;
count = 1;  // OK

if (true) {
  let x = 5;  // block-scoped — only exists in this {}
  var y = 5;  // function-scoped — leaks out!
}
console.log(y);  // 5 (var leaks)
console.log(x);  // ReferenceError
```

**Note on `const`:** The BINDING is constant, but if it points to an object/array, the contents can still mutate:
```js
const arr = [1, 2];
arr.push(3);  // OK — array mutated, but `arr` still refers to same array
arr = [4];    // TypeError — can't reassign const
```

- functions, dates, regex, etc.

**Check type:** `typeof x` returns a string: `'string'`, `'number'`, `'boolean'`, `'undefined'`, `'object'` (for null and arrays — confusing!), `'function'`.

**Loose equality (`==`)** does type coercion. STRICT equality (`===`) doesn't.

```js

0 == false      // true  (false coerced to 0)
```

Summary:
JavaScript is single-threaded — only ONE thing runs at a time. The **event loop** lets async code run without blocking.

**Components:**
1. **Call Stack** — currently executing functions (synchronous)
2. **Web APIs** — `setTimeout`, fetch, DOM events (run outside JS engine)
3. **Task Queue (macrotask)** — `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O callbacks
4. **Microtask Queue** — Promise `.then`/`.catch`, `queueMicrotask`. HIGHER priority than macrotask.

**Algorithm:**
- Run all synchronous code on call stack
- When stack empty, drain ALL microtasks
- Then take ONE macrotask, run it (and its microtasks)
- Repeat

**Why this matters:**
```js
console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));
console.log('4');
// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
```
`1` and `4` are sync. `3` (microtask) runs before `2` (macrotask) even with `0` timeout.

Watch Philip Roberts' "What the heck is the event loop?" talk.

```js
});
```

```js

 .catch(err => console.error(err))
 .finally(() => console.log('done'));      // always runs
```

- `Promise.all([p1, p2])` — wait for ALL to resolve. Rejects if ANY rejects.
- `Promise.allSettled([...])` — wait for all, never rejects. Returns array of `{status, value/reason}`.
- `Promise.race([...])` — first to resolve OR reject wins.
- `Promise.any([...])` — first to RESOLVE (ignores rejections until all reject).
- `Promise.resolve(v)` / `Promise.reject(e)` — instant resolved/rejected.

**Promise chains** flatten async code (vs callback hell):

**Syntax:** between `/` slashes, with flags after:

Summary:
`fetch` is the modern browser API for HTTP requests. Returns a Promise.

**GET (basic):**
```js
const res = await fetch('/api/users');

```

```js
const res = await fetch('/api/users', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Alice' }),
});
```

**Important gotcha:** `fetch` only rejects on NETWORK error — HTTP errors (404, 500) still RESOLVE. Always check `res.ok` or `res.status`.

**Reading response:**
- `res.json()` — parse as JSON
- `res.text()` — raw string
- `res.blob()` — binary
- Each can only be called ONCE

**Cancel a request** with `AbortController`:
```js
const ctrl = new AbortController();
fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal });
ctrl.abort();  // cancels
```

Summary:
`type` aliases create a name for ANY type — primitive, object, union, function, etc. More versatile than `interface` but with subtle differences.

```ts
type ID = string | number;                 // union — interface can't do this
type User = { id: ID; name: string };       // object shape

type Compare = (a: number, b: number) => number;  // function type
```

**`type` vs `interface`:**

| Feature | `type` | `interface` |
|---------|--------|-------------|
| Object shapes | ✅ | ✅ |
| Unions, primitives, tuples | ✅ | ❌ |
| `extends` | via `&` intersection | native `extends` |
| Declaration merging | ❌ | ✅ |
| Better error messages | ✅ (usually) | ⚠️ |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Object shapes that may extend → `interface` (slightly cleaner)
- Unions, complex types, tuples → `type`
- When in doubt → `type`

Summary:
Enums = named constant sets. TypeScript has 2 styles: numeric and string. **PREFER string enums** — better debugging, no auto-increment surprises.

**String enum (preferred):**
```ts
enum Role {
  Admin = 'admin',
  User = 'user',
  Guest = 'guest',
}

function setRole(r: Role) { ... }
setRole(Role.Admin);  // OK
setRole('admin');     // Error — must use Role.Admin
```

**Numeric enum (less safe):**
```ts
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }  // 0, 1, 2, 3
console.log(Direction.Up);  // 0
```

**Modern alternative: union of literals** (often better than enums):
```ts
type Role = 'admin' | 'user' | 'guest';
function setRole(r: Role) { ... }
setRole('admin');   // OK
setRole('boss');    // Error
```

**vs enum:** literal unions are erased at compile time (smaller output), no runtime object created, more flexible. Many modern codebases prefer literal unions over enums.

Summary:
TypeScript ships built-in **utility types** that transform other types. Top picks:

**`Partial<T>`** — make all props optional:
```ts
type User = { id: number; name: string };
type UserUpdate = Partial<User>;  // { id?: number; name?: string }
```

**`Required<T>`** — make all props required (opposite of Partial).

**`Readonly<T>`** — make all props readonly.

**`Pick<T, Keys>`** — pick subset of props:
```ts
type UserSummary = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>;
```

**`Omit<T, Keys>`** — opposite: exclude some keys:
```ts
type UserWithoutId = Omit<User, 'id'>;
```

**`Record<K, V>`** — object type with keys K, values V:
```ts
type RoleMap = Record<'admin' | 'user', string[]>;
// { admin: string[]; user: string[] }
```

**`ReturnType<typeof fn>`** — extract return type of a function.

**`Awaited<T>`** — unwrap Promise type.

**`NonNullable<T>`** — remove `null` and `undefined`.

These avoid repetition and keep types DRY.

Summary:
Migrating an existing JS codebase to TS is INCREMENTAL — no need to rewrite everything at once.

**Step-by-step:**

1. **Install:** `yarn add -D typescript @types/node @types/react ...`
2. **Generate config:** `npx tsc --init` — start with `"allowJs": true, "strict": false`
3. **Rename files** — change `.js` → `.ts` (and `.jsx` → `.tsx`) ONE AT A TIME, top-priority files first
4. **Fix errors** — add type annotations, use `any` temporarily where needed
5. **Tighten gradually:**
   - Turn on `"noImplicitAny"`
   - Then `"strictNullChecks"`
   - Finally full `"strict": true`

- Don't fight TS — when stuck, use `any` or `// @ts-expect-error`, file a "fix later" issue
- Use `@types/*` packages from DefinitelyTyped for JS libraries lacking types
- VS Code's IntelliSense already does some inference even in `.js` — try `// @ts-check` comment at top of a JS file as a stepping stone
- Migration takes WEEKS for large codebases. Plan accordingly.

Summary:
Next.js supports 3 main rendering strategies — pick based on data freshness needs:

**SSG (Static Site Generation):**
- HTML built at BUILD TIME → served from CDN
- Fastest. Best for blog posts, marketing pages, docs
- Triggered by `fetch` with default cache OR no dynamic functions
- `generateStaticParams` for dynamic routes

**SSR (Server-Side Rendering):**
- HTML rendered on EVERY REQUEST on the server
- For personalized pages (user dashboard, auth-gated content)
- Triggered by `cache: 'no-store'` or accessing cookies/headers

**ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration):**
- Generated at build, REVALIDATED in background after N seconds
- Best of both: fast like SSG, fresh like SSR
- Triggered by `next: { revalidate: N }`

**How to choose:**
- Content rarely changes → SSG
- Content changes often + personalized → SSR
- Content changes occasionally, NOT personalized → ISR

**Modern reality (App Router):** Don't pre-decide page-level rendering — Next.js infers per-route based on the data calls you make.

Next.js handles env vars with a critical SERVER-vs-CLIENT distinction.

**Files (loaded automatically):**

```ts
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_SECRET=abc123
```

- DB password, API secret, JWT secret → plain `process.env.X` (server only)

Summary:
**Vue** is a **JavaScript framework for building user interfaces**. It builds on standard HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and adds two superpowers: **declarative rendering** (you describe what the UI should look like based on your data) and **reactivity** (Vue automatically updates the DOM when that data changes).

Modern Vue 3 uses the **Composition API** inside `<script setup>`. The main tool for reactive state is `ref()`, which wraps any value so Vue can track it:

```js
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
console.log(count.value) // 0 — read/write with .value in JS
count.value++            // now 1
```

In **JavaScript code** you read or change a ref through its `.value` property. In the **template**, refs are **auto-unwrapped**, so you just write `{{ count }}` (no `.value`).

There is also `reactive()`, which makes an object itself reactive:

```js
import { reactive } from 'vue'

const state = reactive({ count: 0 })
state.count++ // no .value needed
```

But `reactive()` has real limits: it **only works for object types** (objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`) — never primitives like numbers or strings — you cannot reassign the whole object, and destructuring breaks reactivity. Because of this, the docs recommend **`ref()` as the primary API** for declaring reactive state.

Why `.value`? Plain JavaScript variables cannot be intercepted, but an object's property can — the `.value` getter/setter is what lets Vue know exactly when the value is read or changed.

Summary:
**Vue Router** is the official router for Vue single-page apps — it swaps components in and out as the URL changes, with **no full page reload**.

Create the router with **`createRouter()`** and pick a history mode with **`createWebHistory()`** (HTML5 mode = clean URLs, no `#`). The **`routes`** array maps each URL `path` to a `component`:

```js
import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router'
import Home from './Home.vue'
import About from './About.vue'

const routes = [
  { path: '/', component: Home },
  { path: '/about', component: About },
]

export const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHistory(),
  routes,
})
```

Register it on the app before mounting:

```js
import { createApp } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'

createApp(App).use(router).mount('#app')
```

This globally registers two components:

- **`<router-view>`** — the placeholder that renders whichever component matches the current URL.
- **`<router-link>`** — a replacement for the `<a>` tag used for navigation. Its **`to`** prop sets the destination, and it changes the URL **without reloading** the page:

```vue
<nav>
  <router-link to="/">Home</router-link>
  <router-link to="/about">About</router-link>
</nav>

<router-view />
```

Bootstrap is a **prebuilt component + utility CSS framework**. Unlike Tailwind (where you compose atomic classes), Bootstrap ships ready-made components plus a **12-column grid**. The fastest setup is the official CDN — one CSS link and one JS bundle (the bundle already includes Popper, and **Bootstrap 5 needs no jQuery**): ```html ``` Or install with a package manager: `npm install bootstrap@5.3.8`. The **grid** is Bootstrap's core layout tool and nests three levels: a **`.container`** (or **`.container-fluid`** for full width) wraps one or more **`.row`** elements, and each row holds **columns**. Every row is divided into **12 units**, so `col-6` is half and `col-4` is a third; a bare `.col` splits the space equally. Summary:
Beyond components, Bootstrap also has **utility classes** — small single-purpose helpers, much like Tailwind — for spacing, layout, and color. **Spacing** follows the pattern **`{property}{sides}-{size}`**: - property: `m` (margin) or `p` (padding) - sides: `t` top, `b` bottom, `s` start (left in LTR), `e` end (right in LTR), `x` left+right, `y` top+bottom, or blank for all four sides - size: `0`–`5` on a fixed scale (`0`=0, `1`=.25rem, `2`=.5rem, `3`=1rem, `4`=1.5rem, `5`=3rem), plus `auto` (margins only) ```html
Spaced box
…
``` So `mt-3` is 1rem top margin, `px-2` is .5rem left/right padding, and `me-auto` (margin-right: auto in LTR) pushes later items to the right. **Flexbox** utilities: `.d-flex` (or `.d-inline-flex`) turns on flex; then align with `.justify-content-{start|end|center|between|around|evenly}` (main axis) and `.align-items-{start|end|center|baseline|stretch}` (cross axis); set direction with `.flex-row` / `.flex-column`. **Color** utilities: text with `.text-primary`, `.text-success`, `.text-danger`, `.text-body-secondary`; backgrounds with `.bg-primary`, `.bg-success`, `.bg-light`, `.bg-dark`. Unlike Tailwind's numeric `text-red-500`, Bootstrap colors are **semantic** — primary, success, danger — not a numbered palette.

Summary:
Bootstrap is **mobile-first and responsive by default**. A column class with a breakpoint infix only "kicks in" at that width and up; **below it the column is full width and stacks vertically**. So `col-md-6` renders as two side-by-side halves on tablets/desktops but a single stacked column on phones — pair it with `col-12` to be explicit: ```html
Main
Sidebar
``` Most **utilities are responsive too** — insert a breakpoint infix: `d-none d-md-block` (hidden on phones, shown as block from `md`), `text-sm-center`, `p-lg-5`. **Customizing** Bootstrap happens two ways: 1. **Sass** (compile-time): override variables — each carries a `!default` flag — but you must set them **before** importing Bootstrap: ```scss $primary: #6f42c1; $body-bg: #f8f9fa; @import "bootstrap/scss/bootstrap"; ``` 2. **CSS variables** (runtime): Bootstrap ships custom properties prefixed **`--bs-`**, so you can retheme without recompiling Sass: ```css :root { --bs-primary: #6f42c1; } a { color: var(--bs-primary); } ``` Key ideas: - Columns stack below their breakpoint (mobile-first) - Responsive utilities: `d-md-block`, `text-lg-end`, `m-xl-4` - Sass: override `$primary`, `$body-bg` **before** `@import "bootstrap"` - CSS vars: `--bs-primary`, `--bs-body-bg`, used via `var(--bs-…)`
